lesson.title: An Uneasy Peace: The Treaty That Ended One War and Sowed the Next
lesson.summary: Signed on June 28, 1919, the Treaty of Versailles imposed harsh terms on defeated Germany and created the League of Nations, but the U.S. Senate's refusal to ratify it left Wilson's vision unfulfilled and the settlement's harshness helped set the stage for renewed conflict two decades later.
lesson.body:
The Paris Peace Conference opened in January 1919, bringing together the victorious Allied powers to decide the terms of peace. The most consequential decisions rested with the so-called Big Four: President Wilson representing the United States, Prime Minister David Lloyd George representing Britain, Premier Georges Clemenceau representing France, and Prime Minister Vittorio Orlando representing Italy. Germany itself was excluded from the negotiations and was presented with the finished treaty to accept, not to help write.

The conference quickly exposed the tension described at the end of the previous chapter. Wilson pushed hard for the principles behind his Fourteen Points, especially the creation of a League of Nations and a peace that avoided humiliating or crippling the defeated powers. Clemenceau, representing a France that had lost roughly 1.4 million soldiers and had watched much of its northeastern territory turned into a battlefield, demanded strong security guarantees against future German aggression along with substantial reparations. The treaty that emerged was very much a compromise, and one that left few of its authors fully satisfied.

The Treaty of Versailles was signed on June 28, 1919, in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, symbolically exactly five years after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand that had helped set the war in motion. Its terms were severe. Germany was forced to accept blame for causing the war under what became known as the war guilt clause, and to pay heavy reparations, a final figure set later, in 1921, at 132 billion gold marks. Germany lost significant territory, including Alsace-Lorraine to France and land that helped form the newly reconstituted nation of Poland, and it surrendered its overseas colonies, which were reorganized as League of Nations mandates administered by the victorious powers. The treaty also sharply restricted the German military, capping the army at 100,000 troops and banning an air force and submarines, while demilitarizing the Rhineland along the French border. Wilson's signature achievement, the League of Nations, was formally established by the treaty as well.

Back home, however, Wilson's vision met fierce resistance. Opponents in the U.S. Senate, led by Republican Henry Cabot Lodge, feared that joining the League of Nations, particularly its Article X provision on collective defense, could drag the United States into future foreign wars without full congressional control over the decision. Wilson refused to accept the compromise reservations Lodge and others proposed, instead undertaking a grueling cross-country speaking tour to build public support directly. The strain proved too much: Wilson collapsed in Pueblo, Colorado, in September 1919, and days later suffered a severe stroke that left him incapacitated for months. The Senate ultimately rejected the treaty in votes held in November 1919 and again in March 1920, and the United States never joined the League of Nations it had helped create, instead concluding a separate peace with Germany through a later treaty in 1921. The treaty's punishing terms toward Germany, combined with the absence of the United States from the peace it had helped design, left behind a fragile and resentment-laden settlement, one that many historians view as having contributed to the political and economic turmoil in Germany that helped enable the rise of Hitler and the outbreak of an even more devastating second World War barely two decades later.
